name: Apache Druid
summary: An open-source real-time analytics database that makes Kafka and Kinesis events queryable within seconds and serves fast slice-and-dice queries to dashboards and APIs.
intro: Druid stores each table, called a datasource, as segments: columnar files that each cover one time interval, such as an hour or a day, and ideally hold 300 to 700 MB. Every string column gets a dictionary, the encoded values, and a compressed bitmap for each distinct value, so a filter becomes AND and OR operations on bitmaps. A cluster splits the work across services. The Overlord hands ingestion tasks to Middle Managers, which run each task in its own JVM; for Kafka and Kinesis a supervisor keeps tasks reading partitions, tracking offsets so every event is ingested exactly once, and new rows are queryable as soon as a task has indexed them. Tasks then publish finished segments to deep storage, which Druid doesn’t provide: S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage or HDFS. The Coordinator assigns segments to Historical servers, which download and cache them on local disk, and Brokers split each query across Historicals and running tasks and merge the results. A PostgreSQL or MySQL database holds segment and task metadata, and ZooKeeper handles leader election and service discovery. Rollup is on by default: rows with the same dimension values and the same truncated timestamp are stored as one row.

You query with Druid SQL or native JSON queries over HTTP; batch loads and rewrites use SQL `INSERT` and `REPLACE` statements run by the multi-stage query engine, and segments kept only in deep storage can still be queried, more slowly. Druid 38.0.0, released on 1 October 2026, runs on Java 21 or 25. Druid is free under Apache 2.0. Imply, founded in 2015 by Druid’s original creators, sells Imply Polaris, a managed Druid service on AWS: Starter projects (up to 25 GB) start at $100 a month and Standard at $600, with usage billed by the hour per project size, for example $1.30 an hour for an A.01 project with 100 GB of capacity (list prices, checked 6 October 2026).
strengths: Events from Kafka or Kinesis are queryable within seconds, with exactly-once ingestion based on partition offsets or shard sequence numbers
Time partitioning plus bitmap indexes let filtered queries skip most data, and built-in sketches give fast approximate distinct counts and quantiles on high-cardinality columns
Rollup at ingestion can cut row counts by orders of magnitude for metrics and event counts
Deep storage keeps every segment, so lost servers are rebuilt by downloading again, and cold data can be queried from deep storage instead of adding Historicals
Scales by adding servers: the cluster rebalances segments by itself and is designed to keep serving through configuration changes and upgrades
limits: Many moving parts: Coordinator, Overlord, Broker, Router, Historical and Middle Manager services, plus ZooKeeper, a metadata database and deep storage, each a JVM to size and tune
No updates of single records by primary key and no `UPDATE` statement: you overwrite whole time ranges with `REPLACE` or a reindexing job
Rollup is irreversible: once rows are combined at ingestion, individual events can’t be queried
Joins are limited: the native engine broadcasts every table except the leftmost, which must fit in memory; the Dart engine’s sort-merge joins are still experimental
Streaming and repeated ingestion leave many small or overlapping segments, so compaction has to be set up and watched

sections.title: Druid, Pinot and ClickHouse
sections.intro: The three open-source databases most often compared for user-facing analytics. All are Apache 2.0 licensed; they differ in how many pieces you run, how they pre-aggregate and how they handle changed rows.

rows.label: Built at
values: LinkedIn, for member-facing features such as Who Viewed Profile
Yandex, for the Yandex.Metrica web analytics service

rows.label: Cluster pieces
values: Six service types, plus ZooKeeper, a metadata database and deep storage
Controllers, brokers and servers, coordinated by Apache Helix on ZooKeeper
One binary; replicated clusters add ClickHouse Keeper

rows.label: Pre-aggregation
values: Rollup at ingestion, on by default
Star-tree index of pre-aggregated values across several columns
Incremental materialized views that write into a second table

rows.label: Changing rows
values: No updates by key; overwrite whole time ranges
Mutations and lightweight deletes; not cheap row-level edits

notes: Compiled from each project’s documentation. It says nothing about speed; compare on your own data and queries.

items.name: Self-managed Druid
items.text: Free. Download a release or use the Kubernetes extension to run ingestion tasks as jobs. A single machine for the quickstart needs at least 6 GiB of RAM; production clusters typically run master, query and data servers separately.

items.name: Imply Polaris Starter
items.text: Managed Druid for proofs of concept: projects up to 25 GB, variable performance.

items.name: Imply Polaris Standard
items.text: Production projects up to 9.6 TB, a 99.9% uptime SLA and private networking. Projects are billed hourly by size, from $0.80 an hour (D.04) to $124.80 (A.96).

items.name: Imply Polaris Custom
items.text: Unlimited project size, a 99.95% SLA and scheduled upgrades.

story: Metamarkets sold ad analytics dashboards whose customers wanted to drill into billions of events along any combination of dimensions, in under a second. Over a year it tried Greenplum, InfoBright, MySQL and HBase. Pre-computing every aggregation into a key-value store kept queries fast, but as dimensions grew the batch jobs ran past 24 hours, far too late for fresh data. So in April 2011 Eric Tschetter introduced Druid, a distributed, in-memory OLAP store the company had built itself.

Metamarkets open-sourced Druid in October 2012 under GPLv2, with Netflix evaluating it for real-time monitoring. A 2014 SIGMOD paper by Fangjin Yang, Tschetter, Xavier Léauté, Gian Merlino and colleagues described the design: real-time nodes that hand off immutable segments to deep storage and historical nodes that serve them. The name comes from the shape-shifting druid class in role-playing games.
In February 2015 Druid switched to Apache 2.0 to invite community governance, and that year its creators founded Imply. Druid entered the Apache Incubator in 2018 and graduated in December 2019.

choices.why: Grouping raw impressions by timestamp and the chosen dimensions made Metamarkets’ data set often about 100 times smaller, while still letting users slice it any way at query time.

Historical nodes only read data that never changes, so they give consistent reads and scan segments in parallel without locks. A permanent copy in S3 or HDFS means servers can be replaced by downloading segments again.

choices.choice: Bitmap indexes for every dimension value
choices.why: Users filtered on arbitrary combinations of dimensions. Boolean operations on compressed bitmaps, a technique from search engines, answer those filters without scanning rows.

choices.choice: Separate node types for fresh and historical data
choices.why: Real-time nodes keep recent events in a queryable in-memory index and hand off finished segments, so ingestion and queries over older data scale independently.
